body:
The meaning of Bhakti

Bhakti means devotion or loving dedication to God. In medieval India, many saint-poets taught that sincere devotion, moral conduct and an individual's relationship with the Divine were more important than outward religious display alone.

In Gujarat, these ideas found expression through poems, songs, public storytelling and religious communities. Devotional compositions were often written or sung in Gujarati and other languages understood by ordinary people. This helped religious teachings circulate beyond groups with access to formal Sanskrit learning.

Gujarati Bhakti was not a single organisation or a uniform set of beliefs. Different saints emphasised Krishna or Rama devotion, knowledge of the formless Supreme Reality, criticism of hypocrisy, service to the needy or disciplined community life.

Saguna and Nirguna Bhakti

Two important forms of devotion

Saguna Bhakti is devotion to God understood through recognisable qualities or a personal form, such as Krishna or Rama. Nirguna Bhakti emphasises the Supreme Reality beyond physical form and worldly attributes.

Narsinh Mehta, Meerabai and Dayaram are particularly associated with Krishna devotion. Kabir emphasised a formless Supreme God. Akho's poetry focused strongly on spiritual knowledge and direct understanding of ultimate reality.

These are useful distinctions, but they are not completely separate historical communities. Some Gujarati saint traditions combined the language of personal devotion with teachings about the formless Divine.

Devotional Literature in Gujarati

Poetry and music were central to the spread of Bhakti because listeners could remember and repeat compositions. Several literary forms became associated with particular poets.

Literary formMeaning or featureImportant association
PrabhatiyaDevotional song associated with the morningNarsinh Mehta
PadaShort lyrical verse, often sungNarsinh Mehta and Meerabai
ChhappaUsually a 6-line composition, often used for pointed criticismAkho
GarbiLyrical song expressing devotion and emotionDayaram
AkhyanNarrative poem or story presented in versePremanand Bhatt
ChabkhaForceful verse criticising moral faults and hypocrisyBhoja Bhagat
BhajanGeneral term for a devotional songGanga Sati and many other saints

Religious and Social Influence

Saint-poets influenced Gujarat in several connected ways. Devotional songs enriched Gujarati literature and music. Teachings about compassion and spiritual equality questioned pride based on caste or status. Institutions such as temples, religious congregations and charitable feeding centres gave these beliefs a practical place in community life.

However, a teaching that criticised social discrimination did not necessarily remove discrimination from society. Similarly, all Bhakti saints did not reject rituals, images or established religious institutions. Their individual teachings must be understood separately.

Why These Distinctions Matter

A preliminary examination may associate a person with a literary form, place, religious tradition or social contribution. Identifying the central feature is more reliable than assuming that every saint followed the same path.

Prelims focus

  • Bhakti means devotion or loving dedication to God.
  • Saguna Bhakti focuses on God with a personal form or attributes; Nirguna Bhakti emphasises the formless Supreme Reality.
  • Narsinh Mehta is associated with prabhatiyas, Akho with chhappas and Dayaram with garbis.
  • Premanand Bhatt is associated with akhyan literature and Bhoja Bhagat with chabkhas.
  • Gujarati saint traditions influenced devotional poetry, ethical teachings and community service.
  • Trap: Not every Bhakti saint rejected temple worship or followed Nirguna Bhakti.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts-II, Class 7, chapter 8, Devotional Paths to the Divine, printed pp. 104–115; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part II, theme 6, Bhakti-Sufi Traditions, printed pp. 161–165; Gujarati Vishwakosh, entries Gujarati Poetry and Garbi-Garbo, consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Devotional singing helped religious ideas reach ordinary people in medieval Gujarat.

title: Gujarati Bhakti: Devotion, Language and Social Values

body:
The Poet-Saint of 15th-Century Gujarat

Narsinh Mehta, also called Narsi Mehta or Narsinh Bhagat, was an important Gujarati poet-saint of the 15th century. He is traditionally associated with Talaja in present-day Bhavnagar district and Junagadh in Saurashtra, where he spent a significant part of his life.

He is popularly honoured as the Adi Kavi of Gujarati literature. This is an honorific recognising his foundational importance in Gujarati devotional poetry. It should not be interpreted as proof that no Gujarati poetry existed before him.

Narsinh's compositions circulated widely through singing and oral transmission. Some details of his life and the attribution of individual verses vary across later traditions. For preliminary-level study, his period, region, Krishna devotion and major poetic associations are the most secure identifying features.

Krishna as the Centre of Devotion

Narsinh's poetry expresses intense devotion to Krishna. His songs describe divine love, Krishna's activities and the devotee's longing for closeness to God.

Many compositions attributed to him are padas, or lyrical devotional verses. He is particularly remembered for prabhatiyas, morning devotional songs. Their musical form helped devotional ideas become part of everyday religious life.

The poems could be sung and remembered by people who had not received formal religious education. This connection between local language, music and devotion helped establish his lasting place in Gujarati culture.

Vaishnav Jan To and the Meaning of a True Devotee

The famous bhajan Vaishnav Jan To is traditionally attributed to Narsinh Mehta. Its central teaching is that a true Vaishnava, or devotee of Vishnu, recognises the suffering of others and responds with compassion.

The composition gives ethical conduct an essential place in devotion. A person does not become an ideal devotee merely through outward religious identity; concern for others, humility and freedom from pride are equally important.

The song later became strongly associated with Mahatma Gandhi's prayer gatherings. This is a later historical influence of Narsinh's devotional tradition, not an event from the poet's own lifetime.

Devotion and compassion belong together

Narsinh Mehta's best-known ethical message connects sincere Vaishnava devotion with the ability to understand and relieve the suffering of others.

Social and Cultural Significance

Narsinh's songs helped establish the expressive power of Gujarati as a language of religious poetry. Traditions about his life also emphasise devotion across differences of social status.

Narsinh Mehta no Choro in Junagadh is traditionally associated with his devotional gatherings and forms part of his cultural remembrance.

Narsinh's life also became the subject of later Gujarati narrative poems. The story of Kunvarbai's Mameru, associated with the ceremonial occasion involving his daughter, appears in later literary treatments, including an akhyan by Premanand. Narsinh himself must therefore be distinguished from the poets who later narrated stories about him.

Prelims focus

  • Narsinh Mehta was a Gujarati Krishna-devotee poet of the 15th century.
  • His important geographical associations are Talaja and Junagadh in Saurashtra.
  • He is popularly known as the Adi Kavi of Gujarati literature.
  • Prabhatiyas are an important literary and musical form associated with him.
  • Vaishnav Jan To emphasises compassion and was later associated with Mahatma Gandhi's prayer gatherings.
  • Trap: Kunvarbai's Mameru became a subject of later narrative poetry; Premanand's akhyan is not a work written by Narsinh Mehta.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts-II, Class 7, chapter 8, Devotional Paths to the Divine, printed p. 109; Government of India, Census of India 2011, District Census Handbook, Bhavnagar, section on Narsinh Mehta, printed p. 123; Government of India, Census of India 2011, District Census Handbook, Junagadh, section on Narsinh Mehta, printed p. 128; Gujarati Vishwakosh, entry Gujarat: Religion, Culture and Gujarati Literature, consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Vaishnav Jan To connects devotion with understanding suffering, compassion and humility; outward identity alone is insufficient.
pictures.caption: Narsinh Mehta's devotional ideal connects faith with compassion and humility.

title: Narsinh Mehta: Krishna Bhakti, Compassion and Gujarati Poetry

body:
Meerabai: Devotion Beyond Royal Expectations

Meerabai, also called Mirabai or Mira, was a prominent woman poet-saint associated with the 15th–16th centuries, especially the 16th century. She came from Merta in Marwar, in present-day Rajasthan, and was married into the ruling Sisodia family of Mewar.

Her devotion centred on Krishna, whom she addressed as her beloved Lord, often called Giridhar Gopal. Her songs express personal love, longing and complete dedication to Krishna.

Meerabai is remembered for challenging expectations placed on a royal woman. Her devotional identity took precedence over the conventional demands of courtly life. Traditions about conflicts with her husband's family reflect this tension, although individual dramatic episodes should not all be treated as independently established historical facts.

Meerabai's Spiritual Associations

According to devotional traditions, Ravidas or Raidas, a saint associated with a socially marginalised community, was her spiritual teacher. This association is important because it reflects the challenge that Bhakti could present to the idea that spiritual guidance depended on high social birth. The identification of Ravidas as her teacher should be understood as a traditional account rather than an undisputed biographical fact.

Meerabai's songs were transmitted orally over many generations. Consequently, the exact authorship and wording of every verse attributed to her cannot always be established with certainty.

Meerabai's Connection with Gujarat

Meerabai was not originally from Gujarat. Her principal early-life associations were with Merta and Mewar in Rajasthan.

Nevertheless, she is important to Gujarat's Bhakti heritage because her Krishna devotional songs became popular in Gujarat as well as Rajasthan. Later traditions also connect her travels and final phase of life with Dwarka, the major Krishna pilgrimage centre in Gujarat. Such accounts should be identified as devotional traditions rather than certain records of her movements.

Dayaram: The Gujarati Poet of Garbis

Dayaram (1777–1853) was a major Gujarati Krishna-devotee poet. He was born at Chanod, on the Narmada, and died at Dabhoi, both in present-day Gujarat.

Dayaram belonged to the Pushtimarg, a Vaishnava devotional tradition associated with Vallabhacharya. Pushtimarg places particular importance on loving devotion to Krishna and the devotee's relationship with him.

Dayaram's most characteristic literary contribution was the garbi. His garbis explore Krishna's divine play, Radha's affection, the emotions of the gopis and the experience of separation from the beloved Lord.

In these compositions, devotion is expressed through the language of human love. The emotional relationship between Krishna and his devotees represents spiritual dedication, rather than merely an ordinary romantic story.

Dayaram also wrote Rasikvallabh in 1828. This work explains aspects of Pushtimarg devotional philosophy. His poetry and theological writing therefore belong to the same broad Krishna-centred religious outlook.

How to Distinguish Meerabai and Dayaram

FeatureMeerabaiDayaram
PeriodPrimarily 16th century1777–1853
Main geographical linkMerta and Mewar; songs popular in GujaratChanod and Dabhoi, Gujarat
Devotional focusPersonal surrender to Krishna as Giridhar GopalKrishna devotion within Pushtimarg
Literary associationBhajans and padasGarbis and Rasikvallabh

Both poets expressed Krishna devotion, but they belonged to different periods and contexts. Meerabai was associated with Rajasthan's royal society and became popular in Gujarat; Dayaram was a Gujarati poet closely linked to Pushtimarg and the garbi form.

Prelims focus

  • Meerabai was associated with Merta in Marwar and marriage into Mewar's ruling family.
  • Her chosen deity was Krishna, often addressed as Giridhar Gopal.
  • The tradition linking Meerabai with Ravidas is a traditional spiritual association.
  • Meerabai's songs became popular in Gujarat; Dwarka is connected with later traditions about her life.
  • Dayaram lived from 1777 to 1853 and is associated with Chanod, Dabhoi, Pushtimarg and garbis.
  • Trap: Dayaram's Rasikvallabh dates to 1828; Meerabai should not be identified as a Gujarat-born poet.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts-II, Class 7, chapter 8, Devotional Paths to the Divine, printed pp. 114–115; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part II, theme 6, section 8.3, Mirabai, the Devotee Princess, printed pp. 164–165; Gujarati Vishwakosh, entries Dayaram and Garbi-Garbo, consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Meerabai originated in Rajasthan; her songs became popular in Rajasthan and Gujarat, while Dwarka is linked to later devotional accounts.
pictures.caption: Meerabai's birthplace and marriage associations were in Rajasthan, while her songs became popular in Gujarat.

pictures.alt: An early-19th-century Gujarati family sings devotional garbi in a courtyard, clapping and playing a drum and small cymbals.
pictures.caption: Dayaram's garbis belonged to the living tradition of sung Gujarati Krishna devotion.

title: Meerabai and Dayaram: Two Expressions of Krishna Devotion

body:
Akho: Knowledge as the Basis of Religious Life

Akho, also called Akha Bhagat, was a Gujarati saint-poet of the 17th century. He is associated with Jetalpur and Ahmedabad and is traditionally identified with the goldsmith community.

Akho belongs particularly to the Jnana-margi, or knowledge-oriented, stream of devotional literature. He taught that spiritual understanding must arise from insight and personal experience, rather than dependence on outward religious behaviour alone.

His poetry criticised empty rituals, religious hypocrisy, pride and the tendency to accept appearances without understanding their meaning.

Chhappas and Important Works

Akho is especially remembered for his chhappas, concise poetic compositions commonly arranged in 6 lines. Their sharp observations and memorable language made them effective for questioning social and religious pretence.

His important works include Akhegita (1649) and Guru-Shishya Samvad (1645). These works discuss spiritual understanding, the relationship between individual experience and ultimate reality, and the importance of proper guidance.

Akho respected the role of a spiritual teacher, but his writing also stressed that genuine understanding cannot be replaced by the mere appearance of discipleship.

Premanand Bhatt: The Master of Gujarati Akhyan

Premanand Bhatt was a major Gujarati narrative poet active during the later 17th century. He was associated with Vadodara and is remembered as an outstanding composer and performer of akhyans.

What is an Akhyan?

An akhyan is a sustained narrative poem that presents an episode or story in verse. Unlike a short devotional lyric, it develops characters, events and emotions through storytelling.

Premanand adapted episodes from religious and literary traditions into engaging Gujarati narratives. His works contributed to the popularity of public storytelling and helped audiences understand familiar religious stories through their own language.

Important Works of Premanand

  • Sudamacharitra (1682): A narrative based on the story of Sudama and Krishna.
  • Mameru (1683): An akhyan associated with Narsinh Mehta and the ceremonial occasion involving his daughter Kunvarbai.
  • Okhaharan: A narrative based on a Krishna-related episode.
  • Nalakhyan: A celebrated narrative based on the story of Nala.

Premanand's association with Narsinh Mehta is primarily literary: he retold episodes connected with the earlier saint's life. They were not contemporaries.

Akho and Premanand Were Not the Same Kind of Poet

Akho frequently used short, pointed poetry and philosophical reflection to question superficial religion. Premanand used extended narratives to present religious stories and human emotions. Both strengthened Gujarati literature, but their principal literary forms and purposes were different.

Two Different Figures Named Premanand

Premanand Bhatt was the 17th-century Gujarati akhyan poet. Premanand Swami, also remembered by the name Sakhi, belonged to the later Swaminarayan devotional tradition. These names must not be treated as referring to the same person.

Prelims focus

  • Akho was a 17th-century Gujarati Jnana-margi saint-poet associated with Jetalpur and Ahmedabad.
  • His characteristic form was the chhappa, commonly a 6-line composition.
  • Akhegita was composed in 1649.
  • Premanand Bhatt was a major akhyan poet associated with Vadodara.
  • Sudamacharitra dates to 1682 and Mameru to 1683.
  • Trap: Premanand Bhatt, the akhyan poet, is different from Premanand Swami of the Swaminarayan tradition.

[Sources: Gujarati Vishwakosh, entries Akho, Premanand and Gujarat: Religion, Culture and Gujarati Literature, particularly the sections on 17th-century literature and Swaminarayan poets; consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: A timeline places Akho's philosophical works of 1645 and 1649 before Premanand Bhatt's narrative works of 1682 and 1683.
pictures.caption: Akho's philosophical writing and Premanand's narrative poetry belong to the Gujarati literary tradition of the 17th century.

title: Akho and Premanand: Spiritual Reflection and Narrative Poetry
